AI Server Demand Drives Polarization in MLCC Lead Times, With High-End Products Approaching 10 Months

Korean media reports that MLCC lead times are diverging sharply depending on product specifications.

While supply conditions for general-purpose products remain relatively stable, lead times for high-capacitance, high-end products used in artificial intelligence servers have lengthened significantly.

According to TTI’s lead-time trend chart, as of August, lead times for most standard case-size multilayer ceramic capacitors remain at 14–18 weeks, or approximately 3.5–4.5 months. High-capacitance and high-voltage products have lead times of around 15–20 weeks, or roughly 4–5 months.

Avnet Abacus’s August 2026 lead-time guide similarly lists multilayer surface-mount, high-capacitance, and automotive-grade products at eight to more than 20 weeks, or approximately 2–5 months, with the outlook categorized as stable.

The situation is different for high-end products.

ComponentNews classifies server-grade MLCCs as being at a critical supply level, with lead times of more than 20 weeks—or over five months—for Murata and Samsung Electro-Mechanics products. It expects these conditions to persist through the second half of this year.

DigiKey’s lead-time data also shows significant supplier-to-supplier variation in high-capacitance products, with some Samsung Electro-Mechanics components averaging around 40 weeks. Lead times for Murata’s high-capacitance products of 1 microfarad or more reached as much as 30 weeks in July, up from 24 weeks in June. Some distribution channels have cited lead times of up to 36 weeks.

The main driver of this polarization is surging demand from AI servers and data centers. AI servers require five to 13 times more high-capacitance, compact, and highly reliable MLCCs than conventional servers for power-delivery-network decoupling and filtering.

Korean media emphasizes that lead times of five to more than 10 months for high-end products are likely to persist for the foreseeable future. Unlike in the past, when passive-component lead times moved flexibly with the economic cycle, the current pronounced divergence is being interpreted not as a temporary boom but as a fundamental restructuring of demand centered on AI.

Moreover, new capacity expansions have been pushed back from the fourth quarter of 2026 into 2027, making it difficult to resolve the supply-demand imbalance in the near term. Major manufacturers are simultaneously raising prices and entering into more long-term supply agreements.

Lead times exceeding five months and approaching a full year indicate that manufacturers have reached a point where they cannot quickly increase supply. At the same time, they signal strengthening pricing power and the beginning of a meaningful improvement in profitability driven by a richer mix of high-value products.

Korean media reports that TSMC has secured a technological edge in backside power delivery with A16, putting it a step ahead of Intel and Samsung in the competition.

Specifically, TSMC has successfully developed and validated A16, the industry’s first angstrom-class CMOS platform featuring its Super Power Rail (SPR) backside power delivery scheme.

The key achievement is that A16 retains the gate density and design flexibility enabled by NanoFlex in the existing N2P process, an enhanced version of N2.

In conventional semiconductor chips, both power-delivery interconnects and signal interconnects are placed together on the front side of the chip. As process nodes shrink, however, competition between the two in an increasingly confined space exacerbates routing congestion and increases electrical resistance, leading to more severe voltage-drop, or IR-drop, problems.

Addressing these issues through backside power delivery typically requires substantial changes to transistor placement or cell structures.

These challenges become more pronounced as process nodes shrink. Supplying power from the back side of the chip has generally required designers to give up parts of their existing cell libraries and design expertise.

TSMC has completely separated the power-delivery network from the front-side signal wiring by moving it to the back side of the chip. Power is delivered directly to the source and drain of each transistor through dedicated vertical connections, or VBs. In the process, TSMC has kept the front-side gate structure, cell dimensions, and layout area almost unchanged, preserving compatibility with existing designs.

Intel, by contrast, had already modified its existing cell configuration and redesigned its cell architecture during PowerVia testing, including adjustments to pin counts and the relaxation of metal-pitch requirements. Samsung Electronics is also reportedly working to introduce backside power delivery with its SF2 process, but is said to be likely to pursue an approach similar to Intel’s.

TSMC’s achievement is viewed as a technology that can improve efficiency while reducing design complexity for products such as AI accelerators, which require both high power efficiency and strong performance.

Some thoughts on NVIDIA and Wall Street’s $500 billion financing guarantee:

- This should help prevent GPU sales from taking a hit as hyperscalers face tighter cash flows and may no longer be able to pay for GPUs entirely upfront.

- It should accelerate the expansion of the GPU market’s TAM, and I do not view it as circular financing.

- Calling this circular financing is like criticizing the introduction of auto financing by saying that car companies are effectively buying their own cars.

- Another interesting point to watch is that Wall Street is increasingly starting to view GPUs as recoverable collateral.

I joined X in September 2024, so it took me a little under two years to get here.

Honestly, the past few days have been rough for me.

Someone tried to dig up my personal information, managed to identify some of it, and spread it around.

Lately, whenever I see new replies, I have not always had the courage to read them. I have been afraid of what kind of abuse might be waiting there.

But I also looked through the replies to some of the posts mocking me for my age, and people’s perception of me was much kinder than I had expected. It made me feel proud that I may have contributed something worthwhile to this community and conducted myself reasonably well along the way.

I have also received many encouraging messages in my DMs. I am deeply grateful for them.
I would like to clear up a couple of misunderstandings.

1. Jukan bought 2x leveraged SK Hynix at the top in June?

No. I have held a memory position since January, and the part about buying leveraged Hynix in June was a joke. I do not have the guts to run leverage, and my boss and I make jokes like that sometimes. I had no idea that making that kind of joke publicly would bring this much mockery down on me.

2. Is Jukan merely pretending to be an analyst while doing nothing more than quoting other analysts and news reports?

If you have mostly seen my posts on X, I can understand why you might feel that way. But you can find more of my original research and analysis in Citrini’s institutional reports and on our Substack.

Because I work for a firm, there are limits to how much of that work I can share publicly on X. I hope people can understand that.

As for why I appeared to change my view on memory, I said at the time that my long-term thesis had not changed. Still, many people seem to have interpreted my comments as me turning bearish on memory altogether. That was not my intention, although I accept that I could have expressed myself more clearly.

At that time, with HBM content getting nerfed, I thought that even though this was clearly a supply problem and not a demand problem, people would take it bearishly, so memory stocks could perform poorly from a trading perspective. That is why I wrote what I wrote. But it snowballed into something far bigger than I intended.

If I could go back to that moment, I would not write that post.

Watching people I have never met at all hurl abuse at me is more painful than I expected. I used to think of being an influencer as something trivial, but it turns out to be harder than I ever imagined.

This ended up being a more vulnerable post than I intended.

But I got here because of all of you who have read, shared, and supported my work.

Thank you.

Usually it's Asian AI stocks trading at cheaper multiples than U.S. counterparts.

But $TTMI is a rare exception, and the discount doesn't seem like it will last long, especially given its trading well off its ATH while everything else bounced back hard.

The only US listed pure-play PCB maker trades at just 20x forward earnings vs. a 2x median for Asian competitors, even after printing its first $1B revenue quarter at record margins.

High-end AI circuit boards are the next major hardware bottleneck. As designs push past 50 to 100+ layers, board complexity and ASPs are surging, with PCB content cost going from $35k (in GB300) to $116k (In VR200).

Napkin math:

6,000 expected shipments of VR200 in H2 alone * $116K in PCB content = ∼$700M of PCB content revenue

40% market share of $700M = ∼$300M in revenue for $TTMI, just from one generation of rack. 

Moreover, TTMI is positioned right at the center:

-> Over 40% share on NVIDIA’s VR200 platform
-> 30% share on the LPU inference rack
-> Lead supplier across switch generations for Cisco, Arista, and Mellanox
-> PCB supplier to every major AI player in the market.
->M+N architecture guided for ~$600M in H2 revenue alone

An NVIDIA senior account manager recently confirmed TTMI as one of their top five qualified suppliers, calling the partnership "strong and growing".

TTMI doesn't need to guess which AI chip wins because every architecture needs high-layer boards underneath it.

The crazy part? He made his $4.6B fortune as a retail investor. 

Herbert Wertheim is the greatest retail investor to EVER live. 

Born in Philadelphia at the end of the Depression, he was the son of Jewish immigrants who fled Nazi Germany. In 1945 the family moved to Hollywood, Florida, into an apartment above their bakery. He was dyslexic with an abusive father, and he often left home for stretches fishing in the Everglades with Native Americans. 

At 16 he stood in front of a judge on truancy charges and got a choice: the Navy or state reformatory.

He decided to serve in the Navy and got in to optometry school on scholarship and opened a practice in South Florida. He tinkered at night, and in 1970 he founded Brain Power Inc  and made one of the first neutralizers, a chemical that stripped a tinted lens back to clear, which meant opticians no longer had to stock every color. 

After roughly 50 years, BPI was doing $25 million in revenue and about $10 million of net income by 2019, but he reportedly never tried to scale it aggressively. 

Instead he spent those decades investing the profits in the stock market instead.

He bought $AAPL at the 1980 IPO, and more when it sat at $10 in the 90s. $MSFT at the 1986 IPO, Then $HEI Heico when it traded as low as 33 cents. Sales compounded 16% a year for 28 years. His $5M became more than $800 million and made him the largest individual shareholder.

He got hurt too. A 1982 margin call after Volcker hiked rates cost him $50 million and taught him about using too much leverage. BlackBerry $BB burned him too. He has a rule to sell when a position reverses 25% on him.

Everything else he says he holds forever, out of the same ordinary Fidelity and Schwab accounts you use. 

Forbes found him in 2019 at $2.3 billion and they estimate he's worth $4.6B now. Now 87 years old, he's a Giving Pledge signee who has put over $100 million into the public universities that took him in, with his name on colleges at FIU and Florida. He also won last year's charity auction, a Ferrari SP3 for $27M.

All the money from his car purchases will go to the Ferrari Foundation that funds educational initiatives. RM Sotheby's waived the buyer's premium on the lot, so the full $40M goes to charity.
